title: How to Reduce Allergens in Your Home
h1: How Can You Reduce Allergens in Your Home?
description: Dust, pollen, pet dander and mold can make home feel like the worst place for allergies. Here are practical ways to cut down on allergens in every room.
quick_answer: Keep allergens out, filter what gets in, and control the conditions they like. Use a MERV 11 to 13 filter if your system allows, run a HEPA purifier in the bedroom, wash bedding weekly in hot water, vacuum with a HEPA vacuum, and keep humidity between about 30 and 50 percent to limit dust mites and mold.
body:
Southern California has a long allergy season. With our mild weather, something is usually blooming, and Santa Ana winds can carry pollen and dust for miles. Inside, dust mites, pet dander and mold add to it. You can't make a home allergen-free, but you can make it a lot more comfortable.

What are the most common indoor allergens?

  • Dust mites live in bedding, upholstery and carpet, and thrive in humid air.
  • Pet dander sticks to furniture, carpets and clothing, and stays in the air for a long time.
  • Pollen comes in on clothing, pets and through open windows.
  • Mold spores grow in damp bathrooms, around windows and in HVAC systems with moisture problems.
  • Cockroach and rodent debris can trigger allergies too, especially in attics, crawl spaces and ductwork.

How can your HVAC system help with allergies?

Your heating and cooling system moves all the air in your home through one place, the filter. That makes it one of the best tools you have.

  1. Upgrade the filter. A pleated MERV 11 or 13 filter catches far more pollen, dander and fine dust than a basic fiberglass one. Check with a technician that your system can handle it.
  2. Change it on schedule. Every one to three months, or monthly with pets and during heavy pollen or smoke.
  3. Make sure it fits. Gaps around the edges let allergens slip right past.
  4. Keep ducts clean and sealed. Leaky return ducts in the attic or garage can pull in dust and debris.
  5. Run the fan during high pollen days so air keeps passing through the filter.

For allergy-prone households, our indoor air quality services include media filter upgrades, whole-home air cleaners, UV lights and humidity control.

What can you do room by room?

Bedroom

  • Use dust-mite covers on mattresses and pillows.
  • Wash sheets and pillowcases weekly in hot water.
  • Run a portable HEPA purifier sized for the room, especially at night.
  • Keep pets out of the bedroom if pet allergies are an issue.

Living areas

  • Vacuum at least weekly with a HEPA vacuum.
  • Dust with a damp cloth so dust is trapped rather than spread around.
  • Choose washable throws and cushion covers.
  • Cut down on clutter that collects dust.

Kitchen and bathrooms

  • Run exhaust fans to remove moisture.
  • Fix leaks under sinks quickly.
  • Clean visible mildew from grout and caulk.

How do you keep pollen out?

Keep windows closed on high pollen days and windy days, especially during Santa Anas. Take shoes off at the door, change clothes after time outdoors, and wipe down pets after walks. Showering before bed rinses pollen out of your hair so it doesn't end up on your pillow.

Check pollen forecasts and plan yard work for calmer, lower-pollen days. If you can, have someone else mow and trim.

Why does humidity matter for allergies?

Dust mites and mold both need moisture. Keeping indoor humidity between about 30 and 50 percent makes your home much less friendly to them. Near the coast that often means running a dehumidifier or making sure the AC is removing moisture well. Inland, very dry air during Santa Anas can irritate airways too, so the goal is a steady middle range.

What about pets?

You don't have to give up a pet to manage allergies. Brush and bathe pets regularly, ideally outside or by someone without allergies. Wash pet bedding weekly, keep pets off upholstered furniture where you can, and run a HEPA purifier in rooms where they spend the most time. A tighter filter on the HVAC system helps catch the dander that floats through the house.

When should you look at the bigger picture?

If allergies are worse at home than anywhere else even after these steps, look at the house itself. Dust blowing from vents, musty smells or signs of pests in the attic all point to sources that cleaning alone won't fix. A duct inspection, attic cleanup or moisture repair may be what finally makes the difference. And for ongoing symptoms, talk to your doctor or an allergist, who can tell you exactly what you're reacting to.
faqs: What MERV filter is best for allergies?
MERV 11 to 13 filters catch most pollen, pet dander and fine dust. Ask a technician whether your system can handle a higher rating, since some older systems lose airflow with dense filters.
Do air purifiers help with allergies?
Portable purifiers with true HEPA filters help in the room they're sized for, especially bedrooms. Avoid units that produce ozone.
Does duct cleaning help with allergies?
It can help if your ducts hold dust, dander or pollen, or have had pests or mold. If they're clean, a better filter and humidity control will do more.
How often should I wash bedding to reduce allergens?
Once a week in hot water is a good rule for sheets and pillowcases. Wash blankets and pet bedding regularly too.
